blocks.text: Fuller raises another objection: that there was no reason why eating the ostrich should be forbidden in the Law, since the bird was either wholly unknown to the Jews or at least very rare among them, being one that Pliny calls an African or Ethiopian bird, as far removed as possible from Judaea. But this weapon is empty. For even if we granted that the ostrich is born in Ethiopia alone, it would not follow that it was unknown to the Jews, especially in the age of Moses, when they had long been detained in neighbouring Egypt. For in that part of Ethiopia which is nearest to Egypt, Apollonius is said in Philostratus to have found ostriches. But indeed, who does not know that in Arabia too, which borders on Judaea and Syria, there is a great abundance of ostriches? Diodorus teaches this in express words in book 2, in his description of Arabia: Θηρίων τε πλῆθος ἀλκίμων ὁ προσορίζουσα τῇ Συρίᾳ τρέφει [Thēriōn te plēthos alkimōn ho prosorizousa tē Syria trephei]. The part of Arabia which borders on Syria nourishes an abundance of wild beasts of outstanding strength. In this list, after he has [II, 826] placed lions, leopards and tigers, he says: Φέρει δὲ καὶ ζῶα διφυῆ, καὶ μεμιγμένα ταῖς ἰδέαις, ὧν αἱ μὲν ὀνομαζόμεναι στρουθοκάμηλοι περιειλήφασι τοῖς τύποις μίγματα χηνῶν, καὶ καμήλων [Pherei de kai zōa diphyē, kai memigmena tais ideais, hōn hai men onomazomenai strouthokamēloi perieilēphasi tois typois migmata chēnōn, kai kamēlōn]; It also produces animals of ambiguous nature and twofold form, of which those called ostriches have the appearance of geese and camels mixed together. Hence Xenophon, travelling through Arabia with Cyrus, met near the Euphrates οὐκ ὀλίγοι στρουθοὶ αἱ μεγάλαι [ouk oligoi strouthoi hai megalai], not a few ostriches, as he himself relates in book 1 of the Anabasis. And in Heraclides στρουθοὶ οἱ Ἀράβιοι [strouthoi hoi Arabioi], Arabian ostriches, are counted among the birds that were served to the king of the Persians, as has already been observed above ^{d)}. Moreover we have learned from Pollux that the Arabs used ostrich skins in place of breastplates and shields. Accordingly, in the book of the Notitiae the ostrich is among the insignia of Arabia ^{(6)}. Therefore, if Fuller denies that Ethiopian ostriches were known to the Jews, [col. 229] let him at least admit that the Arabian ones could not have been hidden from them. Above all it is absurd that Fuller will have יענה jaana be the strix [screech owl], an animal, forsooth, much better known to the Jews than the ostrich, indeed plainly fabulous, as is clear even from Pliny, book 11, chapter 39. This is why Hesychius, as emended by us, places it ἐν τοῖς τερατείοις [en tois terateiois], among the prodigious animals, such as the Chimaera, the Centaurs, etc.
